topics.title: Concept and Classification of Overheads
explain: Overheads are indirect costs that cannot be conveniently traced to a specific cost unit.
They are incurred for general output rather than a specific work order.
Classification by function includes Factory, Office & Administrative, and Selling & Distribution overheads.
Classification by nature divides overheads into Fixed, Variable, and Semi-variable costs.
Classification by element covers Indirect Materials, Indirect Employee Costs, and Indirect Expenses.
Classification by control divides costs into Controllable and Uncontrollable costs.

flow.title: Classifying Overheads by Nature
steps: Identify indirect expenditure item
Analyze behavior with output change
Categorize into Fixed, Variable, or Semi-variable
Separate fixed and variable portions of semi-variable cost
Apply suitable budgeting and control methods

topics.example: Factory building rent remains fixed at ₹50,000 per month regardless of whether output is 1,000 units or 2,000 units.
remember: Fixed overheads remain constant in total within a given activity level.
Variable overheads vary in direct proportion to production volume.
Semi-variable overheads contain both fixed and variable elements.
mistakes: Confusing direct expenses with indirect overhead costs.
Assuming fixed overhead per unit stays constant when output changes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a functional classification of overheads?
quiz.why: Factory Overhead is classified according to the production function it performs.

quiz.q: Lubricants and cotton waste used for machine maintenance are examples of:
quiz.why: Lubricants do not form part of the finished product, so they are indirect materials.

topics.title: Allocation, Apportionment & Steps for Overhead Distribution
explain: Cost Allocation is the direct assignment of whole cost items to a specific cost center or department.
Cost Apportionment is the distribution of common overheads to multiple departments using logical bases.
Re-apportionment is transferring service department costs to production departments.
Cost Absorption is recovering accumulated departmental overheads from units produced.
Bases for apportionment include floor area for rent, capital value for depreciation, and worker count for welfare.

flow.title: Steps in Distribution of Overheads
steps: Estimate and collect overheads via standing orders
Allocate identifiable costs to specific departments
Apportion common costs using suitable logical bases
Re-apportion service department costs to production departments
Absorb overheads into individual product costs

topics.example: Charging factory rent based on floor area occupied by each department is Cost Apportionment.
remember: Allocation applies to whole cost items directly traceable to one department.
Apportionment applies to common costs split proportionally among departments.
Primary distribution summary combines allocated and apportioned expenses.
mistakes: Apportioning a cost that could be directly allocated to a single department.
Using wrong apportionment bases like employee count instead of floor area for rent.

quiz.q: The direct assignment of a whole cost item to a specific department is called:
quiz.why: Cost allocation deals with whole items of cost directly identifiable with a single department.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the most suitable base for apportioning factory rent?
quiz.why: Rent is related to space, so floor area is the most logical apportionment base.

topics.title: Re-apportionment of Service Department Expenses
explain: Service departments support production departments but do not manufacture goods directly.
Re-apportionment (secondary distribution) transfers service costs to production departments.
Direct Re-distribution Method apportions costs to production departments only, ignoring inter-service work.
Step Method (non-reciprocal) apportions costs sequentially starting from the department serving maximum others.
Reciprocal Service Methods handle mutual inter-service department services using Simultaneous Equations, Trial & Error, or Repeated Distribution.

flow.title: Selecting Re-apportionment Method
steps: Identify service department interactions
If no reciprocal services exist, use Direct Method
If non-reciprocal sequence exists, use Step Method
If reciprocal services exist, choose Simultaneous Equation or Repeated Distribution
Finalize totals under production departments only

topics.example: If Service Dept X serves Y (10%) and Y serves X (5%), simultaneous equations X = Own + 0.05Y and Y = Own + 0.10X determine true total costs.
remember: Direct method completely ignores service provided by one service department to another.
Step method starts with the service department rendering maximum service to other departments.
Simultaneous Equation method gives exact reciprocal service distribution mathematically.
mistakes: Continuing repeated distribution steps past negligible fractional amounts.
Apportioning service costs back to closed service departments in the step method.

quiz.q: Which method ignores services rendered by one service department to another service department?
quiz.why: Direct re-distribution apportions service department expenses over production departments only.

quiz.q: In the Step Method of re-apportionment, distribution starts with the service department that:
o: Renders services to maximum number of departments
Has the highest direct labor hours
Renders services to production departments only
quiz.why: The sequence begins with the department rendering maximum number of services to other service departments.

topics.title: Methods of Absorbing Overheads & Types of Rates
explain: Overhead Absorption charges departmental overheads to individual cost units or jobs.
Methods include % of Direct Material Cost, % of Prime Cost, % of Direct Labour Cost, Labour Hour Rate, Machine Hour Rate, and Rate Per Unit.
Normal Rate uses actual overheads divided by actual base.
Pre-determined Rate is calculated before the period starts using budgeted figures.
Blanket Rate is a single rate used for the entire factory, while Departmental Rate is calculated per department.

flow.title: Computing Pre-determined Absorption Rate
steps: Estimate total departmental overheads for period
Select suitable base like machine or labor hours
Estimate total capacity/volume of selected base
Divide estimated overheads by estimated base volume
Apply calculated rate to actual units or hours

topics.example: If estimated factory overhead is ₹90,000 and estimated direct labor hours are 1,50,000, the Labour Hour Rate is ₹0.60 per hour.
remember: Pre-determined rate = Budgeted Overheads / Budgeted Base.
Blanket rates are valid only when products pass through all departments uniformly.
Departmental rates are preferred when product mix and departmental machinery vary.
mistakes: Using a Blanket Rate when different products spend unequal time in different departments.
Using material cost percentage when raw material prices fluctuate wildly.

quiz.q: A single overhead absorption rate calculated for the entire factory is known as a:
quiz.why: Blanket rate refers to the computation of one single overhead rate for the whole factory.

quiz.q: Which absorption method is best suited for jobs involving minimal machinery and manual labor?
quiz.why: Labour Hour Rate method fully recognizes time spent in manual operations.

topics.title: Computation of Machine Hour Rate
explain: Machine Hour Rate (MHR) is the total cost of operating a machine for one productive hour.
Expenses are classified into Fixed/Standing Charges (rent, insurance, supervisor salary) and Variable/Machine Expenses (power, repairs, depreciation).
Fixed costs per period are divided by total effective machine hours to find hourly standing charges.
Variable costs per hour are calculated individually based on running time.
Unproductive setup time is deducted to calculate effective productive machine hours.

flow.title: Calculating Machine Hour Rate
steps: Collect all machine-related overhead expenses
Classify into Standing Charges and Variable Costs
Calculate effective productive machine hours
Divide Standing Charges by effective machine hours
Calculate hourly rate for power, repairs, and depreciation
Sum standing and variable rates to get MHR

topics.example: If standing charges per month are ₹97,366 and effective machine hours are 365, fixed rate is ₹266.76/hr. Adding variable costs (₹116.10/hr) yields MHR of ₹382.86.
remember: Effective Machine Hours = Total Hours - Unproductive Setup Time.
Power is calculated only on actual running hours excluding non-power setup hours.
Comprehensive MHR includes machine operator wages.
mistakes: Including unproductive setup hours in power consumption calculations.
Mixing monthly fixed costs with annual machine hours.

quiz.q: How is effective machine hours calculated when setup time is unproductive?
o: Total working hours plus setup time
Total working hours minus unproductive setup time
Total working hours divided by setup time
quiz.why: Unproductive setup time must be subtracted from total hours to get productive machine hours.

quiz.q: Which of the following items is treated as a Machine Variable Expense?
quiz.why: Power consumption varies directly with machine running time.

topics.title: Treatment of Under-Absorption and Over-Absorption of Overheads
explain: Absorbed Overheads = Pre-determined Rate x Actual Base.
Under-absorption occurs when Actual Overheads > Absorbed Overheads (Debit balance).
Over-absorption occurs when Absorbed Overheads > Actual Overheads (Credit balance).
Abnormal causes (defective planning, factory inefficiency) are charged directly to Costing Profit & Loss A/c.
Normal causes and small differences are adjusted using a Supplementary Overhead Rate.
Supplementary Rate = Unabsorbed Normal Overhead / Total Units Produced.

flow.title: Under/Over Absorption Treatment Flow
steps: Calculate Absorbed Overhead = Rate x Actual Base
Determine Variance = Actual Overhead - Absorbed Overhead
Identify reasons for variance (normal vs abnormal)
Charge abnormal variance directly to Costing P&L
Calculate Supplementary Rate for normal variance
Apportion balance to WIP, Finished Goods, and Cost of Sales

topics.example: Actual overhead is ₹4,46,380 and absorbed overhead is ₹3,66,380, giving under-absorption of ₹80,000. If ₹40,000 is due to inefficiency (abnormal), debit ₹40,000 to Costing P&L and charge ₹40,000 to production via supplementary rate.
remember: Under-absorption means under-recovery (cost was under-charged to production).
Over-absorption means over-recovery (cost was over-charged to production).
Supplementary rate applies to equivalent completed units of WIP, Finished Goods, and Cost of Sales.
mistakes: Charging abnormal inefficiency losses to product cost instead of Costing P&L.
Using total units sold instead of total units produced to compute supplementary rate.

quiz.q: If actual overhead incurred is ₹5,00,000 and absorbed overhead is ₹5,40,000, the result is:
quiz.why: Absorbed overhead exceeds actual overhead by ₹40,000, creating over-absorption.

quiz.q: Under-absorption of overheads caused by factory inefficiency should be:
o: Distributed to WIP and Finished Goods using supplementary rate
Debited to Costing Profit and Loss Account
Credited to Costing Profit and Loss Account
quiz.why: Abnormal unabsorbed overheads due to inefficiency are debited directly to Costing P&L.

topics.title: Accounting and Control of Administrative Overheads
explain: Administrative overheads are costs of general management and executive direction.
Three methods of accounting: (a) Apportion between Production and Sales, (b) Charge directly to Costing P&L, (c) Add as a separate cost percentage to Works Cost/Production Cost.
Treating admin overheads as a separate addition to Works Cost is widely accepted.
Because admin overheads are mostly fixed policy costs, short-term control is difficult.
Control methods include Departmental Cost Analysis, Budgetary Control, and Standard Costing.

flow.title: Absorbing Administrative Overheads
steps: Collect general administrative expenses
Select absorption base (e.g., Works Cost)
Compute Admin Absorption % = Admin Cost / Works Cost x 100
Apply % to Works Cost of individual jobs
Add to Works Cost to arrive at Cost of Production/Sales

topics.example: If Works Cost is ₹1,21,200 and Administrative Overhead rate is 25% of Works Cost, admin overhead charged is ₹30,300.
remember: Admin overheads include executive salaries, legal expenses, office rent, and audit fees.
Works Cost is the most common base for absorbing admin overheads.
Fixed admin overheads are controlled primarily through budgets and standards.
mistakes: Including administrative overheads in Prime Cost.
Excluding administrative overheads completely from product cost estimates without justification.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the most common base for absorbing Administrative Overheads?
quiz.why: Administrative overheads are commonly absorbed as a percentage of Works Cost.

quiz.q: Administrative overheads are primarily of what nature?
quiz.why: They arise from management policy decisions and remain fixed irrespective of short-term output.

topics.title: Accounting and Control of Selling and Distribution Overheads
explain: Selling overheads are incurred to promote sales and secure orders (e.g., advertising, sales commission).
Distribution overheads are incurred to deliver finished goods to customers (e.g., warehouse rent, carriage outward).
Absorption bases include Sales Value, Cost of Goods Sold, Gross Profit, or estimated fixed/variable rate per unit.
Primary packing is a production cost, while secondary packing for transport is a distribution overhead.
Control is maintained via Past Performance comparison, Budgetary Control, and Standard Costing.

flow.title: Absorbing Selling & Distribution Overheads
steps: Separate selling expenses from distribution expenses
Classify into fixed and variable components
Apportion fixed costs on bases like storage area or sales volume
Calculate per-unit variable costs like packing or commission %
Add fixed per-unit cost and variable per-unit cost for total absorption

topics.example: Showroom rent is apportioned on average space occupied by each product, while sales commission is charged as 4% of sales value.
remember: Selling overheads create demand; distribution overheads execute order delivery.
Primary packing = Production Cost; Secondary packing = Distribution Overhead.
Sales value is the most logical base for absorbing selling overheads.
mistakes: Treating primary packing as distribution overhead instead of production cost.
Apportioning showroom rent on machine hours instead of floor area.

quiz.q: Secondary packing expenses incurred for safe transportation of goods are treated as:
quiz.why: Secondary packing facilitates logistics and transportation, making it a distribution overhead.

quiz.q: Salesmen commission is best apportioned or calculated based on:
quiz.why: Commission to salesmen is directly linked to sales volume or value generated.

topics.title: Capacity Concepts and Idle Capacity Treatment
explain: Installed/Rated Capacity: Maximum theoretical production capacity based on technical specs.
Practical Capacity: Rated capacity minus unavoidable operational delays (80-90% of rated).
Normal Capacity: Long-term average achievable output considering planned maintenance.
Actual Capacity: Output capacity actually achieved during a specific period.
Normal Idle Capacity = Installed Capacity - Normal Capacity.
Abnormal Idle Capacity = Normal Capacity - Actual Capacity (when actual < normal).
Treatment: Unavoidable idle cost -> Supplementary rate; Avoidable idle cost -> Costing P&L A/c; Seasonal idle cost -> Inflated overhead rates.

flow.title: Determining Normal Capacity
steps: Start with Installed/Rated Capacity
Deduct scheduled preventive maintenance time
Deduct normal shut-down days and holidays
Deduct normal idle time and batch change-overs
Arrive at Normal Capacity

topics.example: If Installed Capacity is 1,00,000 units and scheduled maintenance/holidays reduce capacity by 15,000 units, Normal Capacity is 85,000 units.
remember: Installed capacity is theoretical and rarely achievable in normal operations.
Normal capacity is used as the base for absorbing fixed manufacturing overheads.
Avoidable idle capacity costs are charged directly to Costing P&L Account.
mistakes: Confusing Practical Capacity with Installed Capacity.
Recovering avoidable idle capacity costs from products instead of writing off to P&L.

quiz.q: The theoretical maximum capacity of a plant determined by technical specifications is called:
quiz.why: Installed (or rated) capacity represents the absolute maximum output limit under ideal technical conditions.

quiz.q: How should idle capacity cost due to avoidable reasons like power failure be treated?
o: Charged to Costing Profit and Loss Account
quiz.why: Avoidable idle capacity costs represent abnormal losses and must be debited to Costing P&L.

topics.title: Treatment of Specific Items in Cost Accounting
explain: Interest & Financing Charges: Presented separately as an item under Cost of Sales.
Depreciation: Traced to cost objects using Cause & Effect or Benefit Received (Factory -> Production OH, Office -> Admin OH).
Packing Expenses: Primary -> Production cost; Transport -> Distribution OH; Decorative -> Selling OH.
Fringe Benefits: Recovered as direct labor supplementary rate if large, else included in production overheads.
Removal & Re-erection: Treated as production overhead if normal; charged to P&L if caused by faulty planning.
Bad Debts: Normal trading bad debts -> Selling overhead; Extraordinary bad debts -> Excluded from cost accounts.
Carriage Expenses: Inward -> Direct Material cost; Stores -> Factory OH; Outward -> Distribution OH.
Research & Development: Production research -> Production cost; Market research -> Selling OH; Failed research -> Costing P&L.

flow.title: Classifying Packing Costs
steps: Determine primary objective of packing
If required for product protection/handling -> Production Cost
If required for safe transport to customer -> Distribution Overhead
If required for customer request on specific job -> Direct Job Cost
If required for shelf attraction/advertising -> Selling Overhead

topics.example: Carriage inward on raw materials increases Direct Material Cost, while carriage outward on goods sold is a Distribution Overhead.
remember: Primary packing is a component of Production Cost.
Carriage Inward goes to Direct Material; Carriage Outward goes to Distribution Overhead.
Failed research expenses are charged directly to Costing Profit and Loss Account.
mistakes: Including carriage inward under distribution overheads instead of direct material cost.
Treating night shift allowance for a specific customer's emergency order as general factory overhead.

quiz.q: Cost of primary packing necessary to hold or protect a product is treated as:
quiz.why: Primary packing is essential to make the product finished and usable, so it forms part of production cost.

quiz.q: Carriage inward paid on the purchase of raw materials should be:
quiz.why: Carriage inward directly relates to acquiring raw materials and is added to raw material cost.
